sub: OOP concepts, applications and the OOP process
def: Object-oriented programming is a paradigm that decomposes a system into interacting objects, each binding state to the operations permitted on that state, and organises them through encapsulation, data abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism, dynamic binding and message passing.
exp:
The paradigm is best understood as a reaction to what procedural decomposition could not hold together. In a structured C program the data and the functions that maintain its invariants are separate declarations; nothing in the language stops a fourth module from writing a struct field directly and breaking an invariant the other three depend on. Global data is shared by every function that can see it, so the cost of a change grows with the size of the program. OOP inverts the unit of decomposition: the module boundary is drawn around the data, and the only way in is a member function the class author wrote. Everything else in the paradigm follows from that inversion.

The six features usually enumerated for this syllabus are objects and classes, data abstraction and encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, dynamic binding and message passing. Two of these are routinely conflated and MPSC exploits it. Encapsulation is the mechanical act of binding data together with the functions that operate on it and controlling access to them, which in C++ is the private, protected and public sections. Abstraction is the design act of exposing only the essential characteristics through an interface and suppressing the implementation behind it. A class with all-public data members is abstraction-free but still, technically, a bundle; a class whose private members are exposed one-for-one through trivial getters and setters is encapsulated but has abstracted nothing. Dynamic binding is the property that the call bound to a given invocation is resolved by the run-time type of the object rather than the static type of the expression, and in C++ it is opt-in through the virtual keyword.

The process of OOP is a sequence of phases and questions about it are phrased as phase attribution. Object-oriented analysis identifies the entities in the problem domain, their attributes and their responsibilities, and states them without committing to any implementation, language or data structure. Object-oriented design turns that model into a solution-domain structure: class hierarchies, interfaces, the collaborations between objects, the choice of which relationships are inheritance and which are containment. Object-oriented implementation writes that design in a language such as C++, and object-oriented testing exercises it, typically class by class and then by interaction. The line the examiner tests is the analysis-design boundary: if the stem says nothing about implementation and speaks of problem-domain entities and their responsibilities, the answer is analysis, not design.

Relationship choice is the other design question that appears as a one-step reasoning item. Public inheritance asserts is-a and should be used only when a derived object is substitutable everywhere a base object is expected. Composition, where one class holds another as a data member, asserts has-a. A Car needs an Engine's behaviour but a Car is not a kind of Engine, so the design is composition, and inheriting Engine into Car would let a Car be passed to any function expecting an Engine, which is nonsense. The standard aggregation-versus-composition refinement is that composition implies the part's lifetime is owned by the whole, aggregation that it is not.

The named applications are worth memorising in the textbook's own list because a recall item can ask for them directly: real-time systems, simulation and modelling, object-oriented databases, hypertext and hypermedia, AI and expert systems, neural networks, decision support and office automation, and CIM/CAM/CAD systems. Historically Simula 67 introduced classes and objects and Smalltalk made the paradigm popular; C++ was developed by Bjarne Stroustrup at AT&T Bell Laboratories as C with classes.

Exam shape: in the MCQ half this leaf supplies definition-matching items on the four pillars and phase-attribution items on the process. In the conventional half it is one of the most reliably essay-shaped leaves in the unit, because a question of the form compare procedure-oriented programming with object-oriented programming, or explain the features of OOP with examples, can be set every year without repeating itself. Marks are lost by listing features without distinguishing them; write abstraction and encapsulation as two sentences that could not be swapped.
facts: The six features usually listed for OOP are objects and classes, data abstraction and encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, dynamic binding, and message passing.
Encapsulation binds data to the functions that operate on it and controls access; abstraction exposes only essential features through an interface and hides the implementation.

Object-oriented analysis identifies problem-domain entities and their responsibilities with no commitment to implementation; object-oriented design maps that model onto classes, hierarchies and collaborations in the solution domain.
Public inheritance models is-a and requires substitutability; composition, holding one object as a data member of another, models has-a.
Composition implies the containing object owns the part's lifetime; aggregation does not.
Dynamic binding means a call is resolved by the object's run-time type, and in C++ it must be requested explicitly with virtual rather than being the default.
Simula 67 introduced classes and objects; C++ was developed by Bjarne Stroustrup at AT&T Bell Laboratories, originally as C with classes.
Objects communicate by message passing, which in C++ is concretely the invocation of a member function on a receiver object with parameters.
traps: The abstraction-versus-encapsulation swap: a distractor that says abstraction restricts access to members while encapsulation presents a simplified interface has the two definitions exactly the wrong way round, and it is the most common wrong answer on this leaf.

A stem that describes naming the entities of the problem domain and their responsibilities without any implementation commitment is object-oriented analysis; candidates read the word responsibilities as class design and answer object-oriented design.

Needing another class's behaviour is not a reason to inherit from it. If the sentence 'a Car is a kind of Engine' is false, public inheritance is wrong however convenient the reuse; the answer is composition.
mnem: A PIE with a lid: Abstraction, Polymorphism, Inheritance, Encapsulation. Abstraction is the view from outside, encapsulation is the lid that enforces it.

sub: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation
def: A class is a user-defined type that groups data members with the member functions that operate on them under access control; an object is an instance of that type, occupying storage for its own non-static data members while sharing one copy of the class's member function code.
exp:
The storage model is the part of this leaf that carries the marks, because almost every question on it reduces to what is per-object and what is per-class. Member function code is generated once for the whole class and is not part of any object's layout. Non-static data members are per-object: every instance gets its own copy. Static data members are per-class, exist even when no object has been created, and must be defined once outside the class body at namespace scope, because the in-class declaration is only a declaration. So the size of an object is the sum of its non-static data members plus any padding the alignment rules insert, plus one hidden vptr if the class or a base has a virtual function. A class with no data members still has size at least 1 byte, because the language guarantees that two distinct objects have distinct addresses.

A member function knows which object it was called on because the compiler passes a hidden pointer to the receiver as an implicit first argument, available inside the body as this. this is a const pointer to the object type, and const on the member function makes the pointed-to object const, which is why a const member function cannot modify data members that are not declared mutable. The this pointer is also what gives C++ open recursion: a member function that calls another member function of the same object is really calling it through this, so if that second function is virtual and the object is actually of a derived type, the derived override runs. That is the property the term open recursion names, and it is why a base class template method can be customised by a derived class. Static member functions have no this pointer, may therefore only touch static members, and are called as ClassName::f().

Member functions can be defined inside the class body or outside it. Defined inside, the function is implicitly inline. Defined outside, the header is repeated with the class name and the scope resolution operator, as in void Stack::push(int v) { ... }, and it is not inline unless you say inline. Access specifiers are private, protected and public, may appear any number of times and in any order, and the default is private for class and public for struct, which is the only real difference between the two keywords in C++. A friend function or friend class is granted access to private and protected members but is not a member: it has no this pointer and friendship is neither inherited nor reciprocal nor transitive.

Memory for objects is obtained in one of three ways and the distinction is examinable. An object declared inside a function is automatic: constructed where the declaration is reached, destroyed when the enclosing block exits, in reverse order of construction. An object created with new is dynamic: the allocation function operator new obtains raw storage, the constructor then runs on it, and nothing destroys it until delete is applied, which runs the destructor and then operator delete. A static or global object is constructed before main for that translation unit's statics and destroyed after main returns.

An array of objects allocates the elements contiguously and constructs them in index order 0, 1, 2 and so on; they are destroyed in reverse index order. Declaring Item stock[10]; requires Item to have a default constructor, or the declaration will not compile, and this is a favourite trap because the class in the stem has only a parameterised constructor. A brace initialiser list, Item stock[3] = { Item(1), Item(2), Item(3) };, supplies arguments element by element and removes the requirement. An array allocated with new[] must be released with delete[]; using plain delete on it destroys only the first element and is undefined behaviour.

Exam shape: the MCQ items here are storage questions (what does sizeof report, what is shared between objects, which member can a static function touch) and this-pointer questions. In the conventional half this leaf is essay-shaped as write a class with a given specification, define its member functions outside the class body, and demonstrate an array of that class, so practise writing the out-of-class definition syntax by hand rather than only recognising it.
facts: Each object has its own copy of the non-static data members; member function code exists once per class, not once per object, and does not contribute to sizeof.
A static data member is shared by all objects, exists before any object is created, and must be defined once outside the class body in addition to being declared inside it.
sizeof an object with no data members is at least 1, so that distinct objects have distinct addresses; a class with virtual functions additionally carries a hidden vptr.
this is an implicit const pointer to the receiver object passed to every non-static member function; static member functions have no this pointer and can access only static members.
Open recursion is the ability of a member function to invoke another member function on the same object through this, which lets a derived override be selected when that function is virtual.
A member function defined inside the class body is implicitly inline; defined outside, it uses the class name with the scope resolution operator and is not inline by default.
The default access is private for class and public for struct; this is essentially the only difference between the two keywords.
Elements of an array of objects are constructed in ascending index order and destroyed in descending index order; the plain declaration requires an accessible default constructor.
Friendship is granted by the class, is not inherited, not reciprocal and not transitive, and a friend function has no this pointer.
traps: Objects do not each carry a copy of the member functions. A distractor claiming that sizeof grows with the number of member functions, or that each object stores its own code, is wrong; only data members, padding and any vptr count.

Open recursion is the this pointer, not pointers in general and not the parameterised constructor. The term is about self-reference enabling a virtual call back into the derived class, so a distractor offering 'use of pointers' is a near miss by design.
An array declared as Item a[10]; needs a default constructor. If the class in the stem declares only Item(int), the declaration is a compile error, not a run-time one.
Memory allocated with new[] must be freed with delete[]. Writing delete on an array pointer is undefined behaviour, not merely a leak of the later elements.
mnem: Data per object, code per class, statics per class and one vptr if anything is virtual.
rel: Constructors and destructors
OOP concepts, applications and the OOP process
Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects

def: A constructor is a member function with the same name as its class and no return type, run automatically when an object is created, to establish the object's invariants; a destructor is the single member function named with a tilde and the class name, taking no arguments, run automatically when the object's lifetime ends, to release what the object owns.
exp:
Both exist because C++ ties resource management to object lifetime. The constructor is the only point at which an object is guaranteed not yet visible to anyone else, so it is where invariants are established; the destructor is the only point guaranteed to run on every exit path from a scope, including one taken by a thrown exception, so it is where they are released. That pairing is the RAII idiom, and it is why file handles, locks and heap buffers in idiomatic C++ are owned by objects rather than freed by hand.

The forms of constructor are the default constructor (callable with no arguments, either declared with an empty parameter list or with defaults for every parameter), the parameterised constructor, the copy constructor X(const X&), and since C++11 the move constructor X(X&&) and delegating constructors that call a sibling constructor from their own initialiser list. A constructor has no return type, not even void; it can be overloaded, can take default arguments, and cannot be virtual, because selecting the function requires an object that does not exist yet. The copy constructor must take its parameter by reference: taking it by value would require a copy in order to make a copy, so the declaration is ill-formed. A single-argument constructor also serves as an implicit conversion from its argument type, which is why explicit exists.

Order is the single most examined thing here, and it is fixed by the language, not by the programmer. On construction: virtual base subobjects first, then direct base classes in the order they are listed in the derivation, then non-static data members in the order they are declared in the class body, then the constructor's own body. The order of members is their declaration order and not the order you wrote them in the member-initialiser list; writing them out of order compiles but initialises them in declaration order anyway, which is a real source of reading-uninitialised-member bugs. Destruction is exactly the reverse: the destructor body runs first, then members in reverse declaration order, then bases in reverse order.

Trace the standard exam fragment. Given struct A with a destructor printing A, struct B with a destructor printing B, and struct C declaring A a; B b; and a destructor printing C, the statement C c; in main constructs a, then b, then runs C's body. At the closing brace, C's destructor body runs and prints C, then b is destroyed and prints B, then a is destroyed and prints A. The output is CBA. Note that if the question had asked for constructor output with the same shape, the answer would be ABC: the members lead going in and trail coming out.

The member-initialiser list is not merely a style preference. A const data member, a reference data member and a base or member whose type has no default constructor cannot be assigned in the constructor body, because by the time the body runs they have already been initialised or, for a reference, would have to be rebound, which references do not permit. The precise 2026-accurate statement is that such a member must be initialised rather than assigned; since C++11 a default member initialiser written at the point of declaration, as in int& r = someGlobal;, satisfies that requirement without appearing in any initialiser list. So the true claim is 'initialised, not assigned', and the absolute claim 'must appear in the member-initialiser list' is false.

Destructors are where polymorphic ownership goes wrong. If a base class pointer holds a dynamically allocated derived object and delete is applied to that pointer, the derived destructor runs only if the base class destructor is declared virtual; otherwise the behaviour is undefined and in practice only the base part is destroyed, leaking whatever the derived class owned. Declaring the derived destructor virtual does nothing on its own, because the call is dispatched through the static type of the pointer, which is the base. The rule is therefore: any class intended to be deleted through a base pointer gives its destructor virtual, and a pure virtual destructor is legal but must still be given a definition, since the derived destructor will call it.

Exam shape: MCQ items are order-of-execution traces and the virtual-destructor rule. The conventional half asks you to write a class with a default, a parameterised and a copy constructor and explain when each is invoked, or to explain the rule of three, so this leaf is code-writing examinable, not just recall.
facts: A constructor has the same name as its class, has no return type at all, is invoked automatically on object creation, can be overloaded, and cannot be virtual.
A class has exactly one destructor; it takes no arguments, returns nothing, cannot be overloaded, and can and often should be virtual.
The copy constructor's parameter must be a reference, conventionally const X&, because passing by value would itself require a copy.
Construction order is virtual bases, then direct bases in derivation order, then non-static members in class declaration order, then the constructor body; destruction is exactly the reverse.
Non-static members are initialised in the order they are declared in the class, regardless of the order written in the member-initialiser list.
Deleting a derived object through a base class pointer runs the derived destructor only if the base class destructor is virtual; making only the derived destructor virtual has no effect.
A pure virtual destructor is permitted but must still be supplied with a definition, because each derived destructor calls it.
const members, reference members and members of a type without a default constructor must be initialised rather than assigned, which since C++11 a default member initialiser can also satisfy.
If a class needs a user-written destructor it almost certainly also needs a user-written copy constructor and copy assignment operator, which is the rule of three.
traps: Constructor order versus destructor order for a class with member subobjects: members are constructed before the enclosing constructor's body and destroyed after the enclosing destructor's body, so a class C holding A a; B b; prints ABC on the way in and CBA on the way out, not CAB or ABC both times.

For polymorphic delete it is the base destructor that must be virtual, not the derived one. The distractor naming the derived class destructor is deliberately placed to catch candidates who remember only the word virtual.

'Must appear in the member-initialiser list' is too strong for a reference or const member. The correct statement is that it must be initialised rather than assigned in the constructor body, and a default member initialiser at the declaration is an equally valid way to do it.
A member-initialiser list written in a different order from the declarations does not change the initialisation order; the compiler will warn but the run-time order stays declaration order.

A pointer member and a reference member are not interchangeable in this rule. A pointer member can perfectly well be assigned inside the constructor body, so if a stem asks which member cannot be, the answer is the reference.
mnem: Members first in, last out: the constructor body is the last thing to run and the destructor body is the first.

def: Polymorphism is the ability of one interface to select among several implementations; in C++ it is compile-time when the choice is made from the static types of the arguments, as with function and operator overloading and templates, and run-time when it is made from the dynamic type of the object, as with virtual functions.
exp:
The clean way to hold this leaf is to ask when the choice is made. Overloading resolves at compile time: the compiler sees the argument types written at the call site, ranks the candidate functions, and encodes the winner's signature into the mangled symbol name. Virtual dispatch resolves at run time from the object itself. Both are polymorphism, which is why an exam item asking for the type of polymorphism that overloading provides wants compile-time, static or early binding, never run-time.

Function overloading permits several functions of the same name in the same scope provided their parameter lists differ in number, in type, or in the order of types. The return type is not part of the signature for this purpose, so two functions differing only in return type are a redeclaration error, not an overload. For member functions the const qualification is part of the signature, so a const and a non-const version of the same function are a legal overload pair and the compiler picks by the constness of the object. Two classic ambiguity sources are worth remembering: an overload set combined with default arguments, where f(int, int = 0) and f(int) make f(5) ambiguous, and a call whose argument needs a conversion that two candidates accept equally well, such as passing a literal 1 where both f(long) and f(double) exist.

Operator overloading gives an operator a meaning for a user-defined type. The function is named with the keyword operator followed by the symbol, so a Complex addition is Complex operator+(const Complex& rhs) const;. It can be a member function or a non-member, usually a friend so it can reach private members. The arity bookkeeping is where marks are lost, so learn the table rather than deriving it under pressure. A unary operator as a member takes no argument, because the single operand is the object the function is called on; as a non-member it takes one. A binary operator as a member takes one argument, the right-hand operand, the left-hand one being the object; as a non-member it takes two. In every case the non-member form takes one more parameter than the member form, because the member form gets the left operand through this.

Increment and decrement break this pattern in a way that is asked directly. Prefix and postfix have the same symbol, so the language distinguishes them with a dummy int parameter that is never used and is never given a name. As a member, prefix is T& operator++(); with no argument, and postfix is T operator++(int); with one argument, that dummy. As a non-member the counts become one and two. Note also the conventional return types: prefix increments and returns a reference to the modified object, while postfix must take a copy of the old value, increment the object, and return that copy by value, which is why postfix is the more expensive of the two.

The limitations are a recall item in their own right and are best memorised as a list. You cannot create a new operator symbol such as ** or a new spelling of an existing one. You cannot change an operator's precedence, its associativity, or its arity, so a binary operator stays binary. You cannot change the meaning of an operator for the built-in types, which follows from the requirement that at least one operand be of a class or enumeration type; int operator+(int, int) is not allowed. An overloaded operator function cannot have default arguments, with operator() the one exception. Five operators cannot be overloaded at all: the member access dot, the pointer-to-member dot-star, the scope resolution operator, the conditional or ternary operator, and sizeof. Four must be members if they are overloaded at all: assignment, the function call operator, the subscript operator and the class member access arrow. The stream operators are the mirror image: since the left operand of cout << obj is an ostream and not your class, operator<< and operator>> must be non-member functions, conventionally friends, taking the stream by reference and returning it by reference so that the calls can chain.

Exam shape: MCQ items on this leaf are arity counts, the cannot-be-overloaded list and the compile-time versus run-time attribution. The conventional half asks for a complete class with overloaded operators, most often a Complex or a Matrix with plus, an insertion operator and either both increment forms or a subscript, so write out the signatures by hand until the member and friend parameter counts come without thinking.
facts: Function and operator overloading are compile-time, static or early-bound polymorphism; virtual functions are run-time, dynamic or late-bound polymorphism.
Overloads must differ in the number, type or order of parameters; a difference in return type alone is not an overload and is a compile error.
For member functions the const qualifier is part of the signature, so const and non-const versions of the same function form a valid overload pair.
A unary operator overloaded as a member takes no argument; overloaded as a non-member or friend it takes one.
A binary operator overloaded as a member takes one argument; overloaded as a non-member or friend it takes two. The non-member form always takes one parameter more than the member form.
Postfix increment and decrement are distinguished from the prefix forms by an unnamed dummy int parameter, so postfix as a member function takes one argument while prefix as a member takes none.
Prefix increment conventionally returns a reference to the modified object; postfix returns the old value by value and is therefore costlier.
The operators that cannot be overloaded are the member access dot, the pointer-to-member dot-star, the scope resolution operator, the conditional operator and sizeof.
The operators that must be overloaded as member functions are assignment, the function call operator, the subscript operator and the class member access arrow.
An overloaded operator cannot have default arguments, except for the function call operator, and cannot change the operator's precedence, associativity or number of operands.
operator<< and operator>> must be non-member functions because their left operand is a stream object, and they return the stream by reference so that calls chain.
traps: Postfix as a member function takes one argument, not none. Candidates reason that the operand is the object and answer 'no argument', forgetting the dummy int that exists purely to distinguish postfix from prefix; 'no argument' is the correct answer only for prefix as a member.
Overloading is not run-time polymorphism. A question asking which mechanism gives run-time polymorphism wants virtual functions, and overloading is the compile-time distractor placed against it.

Return type alone does not overload a function, but the const qualifier on a member function does. A distractor pairing int f() with double f() is a redeclaration error, while int f() const alongside int f() is legal.

Overloading cannot change precedence or arity. A stem proposing to make a user-defined operator+ bind more tightly than operator*, or to give a binary operator three operands, is describing something the language forbids.

'At least one operand must be of user-defined type' rules out redefining arithmetic for the built-in types, which is a different claim from the cannot-be-overloaded list of five operators; questions mix the two lists.
mnem: Cannot overload: dot, dot-star, double-colon, question-colon, sizeof. Must be members: assign, call, subscript, arrow.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
def: Inheritance derives a new class from one or more existing classes so that the derived class acquires their members and can extend or specialise them; a virtual function is a member function whose call, made through a pointer or reference to a base class, is resolved from the object's run-time type rather than the expression's static type.
exp:
Inheritance is classified by the shape of the derivation graph, and the five names are recall items. Single inheritance is one base and one derived. Multilevel is a chain, A to B to C, where each class is derived from the previous one. Hierarchical is one base with several independent derived classes. Multiple inheritance is one derived class with two or more direct bases. Hybrid, sometimes called multipath, combines these, and the diamond in which D derives from B and C which both derive from A is its standard example. C++ supports all of them. Java deliberately does not: a Java class extends exactly one superclass, so multiple inheritance of classes is absent and only multiple interface implementation is offered, which is why Java is the answer when a stem asks which language does not support all four types.

The diamond creates two problems that virtual inheritance solves together. Without it, D contains two separate A subobjects, so a reference to an inherited member of A is ambiguous and must be disambiguated with the scope resolution operator, and any state in A is duplicated. Declaring the intermediate derivations virtual, as class B : virtual public A, makes the compiler share a single A subobject among all paths. The rule that follows and that examiners like is that a virtual base subobject is initialised by the most derived class in the hierarchy, not by the intermediate classes, and it is constructed before any non-virtual base.

Visibility is governed by a table worth reproducing from memory. A private member of the base is never accessible in the derived class, whatever the mode of derivation; only the base's own members and friends can touch it, and protected exists precisely to give derived classes controlled access. Under public derivation, public members of the base stay public in the derived class and protected stay protected. Under protected derivation, both public and protected members of the base become protected in the derived class. Under private derivation, both become private, so they are available inside the derived class but not to anything further derived from it. The default derivation access, if you omit the keyword, is private for class and public for struct, which catches people who write class D : B and expect an is-a relationship.

Dynamic dispatch works through one indirection. A class that declares or inherits a virtual function gets a vtable, a per-class array of function pointers, and every object of that class carries a hidden vptr to its class's vtable, installed as each constructor runs. A call through a base pointer loads the vptr, indexes the slot for that function, and calls what it finds, so the derived override runs. Two consequences appear as questions. First, because the vptr is set to the current class's table while that class's constructor is running, a virtual call made inside a constructor or destructor dispatches to the version belonging to the class whose constructor or destructor is executing, never to a more derived override. Second, dispatch requires an object accessed indirectly: assigning a derived object to a base object by value slices it, copying only the base subobject and taking the base's vptr with it, so no polymorphism survives. Pointers and references preserve it; values do not.

A pure virtual function is written with the = 0 specifier and declares an interface without an implementation. Any class containing one, inherited or declared, is abstract: it cannot be instantiated, though pointers and references to it are perfectly legal and are the normal way to hold a polymorphic object. A derived class that fails to override every pure virtual it inherits is itself still abstract. The idiomatic use is the shape hierarchy, an abstract Shape with virtual double area() const = 0; and a virtual destructor, with Circle and Rectangle overriding area, and a container of Shape pointers over which one loop computes every area. Since C++11 write override on the derived declaration so that a signature mismatch is a compile error instead of a silently unrelated function, and final where further overriding must be forbidden.

Pointers to objects behave like pointers to any type with two additions. An implicit upcast converts a derived pointer to a base pointer, since a derived object contains a base subobject; the reverse downcast is not implicit and needs dynamic_cast, which is checked at run time and requires the base to be polymorphic, meaning it has at least one virtual function, returning a null pointer on failure for pointers and throwing std::bad_cast for references. Also beware that a derived class member function with the same name as a base one hides every base overload of that name, whatever the parameter lists, and the fix is a using declaration naming the base function in the derived class.

Exam shape: MCQ items are the inheritance-type and access-table recall, the virtual destructor rule and the slicing trap. The conventional half is squarely essay-shaped here, since implement an abstract base class with pure virtual functions and demonstrate run-time polymorphism is one of the most predictable long questions in this unit; the syllabus phrase 'pure Virtual Functions and its implementation in program' is explicit that code is expected.
facts: The types of inheritance are single, multiple, multilevel, hierarchical and hybrid or multipath; C++ supports all of them while Java has no multiple inheritance of classes, only of interfaces.
A private member of a base class is inaccessible in every derived class regardless of the derivation mode; protected members are accessible in derived classes but not to outside code.
Under public derivation base public stays public and base protected stays protected; under protected derivation both become protected; under private derivation both become private.
If the derivation access specifier is omitted, it defaults to private for a class and public for a struct.
In a diamond, declaring the intermediate bases virtual gives a single shared base subobject, and that virtual base is initialised by the most derived class and constructed before non-virtual bases.
A polymorphic class has a per-class vtable and each of its objects carries a vptr; the vptr is set by each constructor as it runs.
A virtual call made from inside a constructor or destructor invokes the version belonging to the class currently being constructed or destroyed, not a derived override.
Assigning a derived object to a base object by value slices it, discarding the derived part and defeating dynamic dispatch; polymorphism requires a base pointer or reference.
A class with any unoverridden pure virtual function is abstract and cannot be instantiated, but pointers and references to it are legal.
dynamic_cast requires a polymorphic base, returns a null pointer on a failed pointer cast and throws std::bad_cast on a failed reference cast.
A derived class member function hides all base class overloads of the same name irrespective of signature; a using declaration brings them back into scope.
traps: Java versus C++ on inheritance types: Java is the language that does not support all four, because it forbids multiple inheritance of classes. Candidates who think of Java's interfaces as multiple inheritance pick C++ or Smalltalk instead.

Overriding and hiding are different. A derived function with the same name but a different parameter list does not override the virtual function; it hides it, and calls through a base pointer still reach the base version. Writing override turns that mistake into a compile error.

A virtual function called inside a constructor does not dispatch to the derived override, so the classic 'call init() from the base constructor to get the derived initialisation' design silently runs the base version.

Private inheritance is not a weaker form of is-a; it models implemented-in-terms-of and no implicit conversion from derived to base is available outside the class, so a base pointer cannot even be formed by outside code.

An abstract class cannot be instantiated but can perfectly well have a constructor, data members and non-pure virtual functions; a distractor claiming an abstract class may contain only pure virtual functions is wrong.
mnem: Single, Multilevel, Multiple, Hierarchical, Hybrid. Pointers and references keep polymorphism; values slice it away.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP
def: A stream is an object representing a sequence of bytes flowing to or from a device, and C++ performs all input and output through a class hierarchy of such objects, with ifstream, ofstream and fstream binding that interface to a file so that the same insertion and extraction operators work on files, the console and strings alike.
exp:
The design is the reason streams are on an OOP syllabus at all. ios_base and basic_ios hold the formatting state and the error state; istream adds the extraction operator and the unformatted input functions, ostream adds insertion and unformatted output, and iostream inherits both. The file classes then derive from those and attach a filebuf: ifstream from istream, ofstream from ostream, fstream from iostream. Because the operators are overloaded functions rather than a fixed format language, writing an operator<< for your own class makes that class printable to cout, to a file and to an ostringstream with no further work, which is polymorphism and operator overloading doing real work rather than a textbook demonstration. The predefined objects are cin, cout, cerr, which is unit-buffered so diagnostics appear immediately, and clog, which is buffered. Include iostream for the console objects, fstream for files, iomanip for the parameterised manipulators and sstream for string streams.

Formatting is stream state, not per-call, and the exception is examined. setw and the equivalent width() apply to the very next insertion only and then reset to zero; precision(), fill() and the flags set through setf, such as fixed, scientific, hex and left, persist until changed. endl inserts a newline and flushes, so in a loop writing many lines it is measurably slower than inserting a newline character, and the flush is the only difference.

A file is opened by the constructor or by a later call to open(), and the mode flags are combined with the bitwise or. ios::in and ios::out select direction, ios::app forces every write to the end of the file regardless of where the pointer is, ios::ate seeks to the end once at open time and then leaves the pointer free to move, ios::trunc discards existing contents, and ios::binary suppresses any newline translation. The defaults are worth knowing exactly: ifstream defaults to in, ofstream defaults to out combined with trunc, and fstream defaults to in combined with out, which does not truncate but does require the file to exist. The subtlety that catches even experienced candidates is that truncation is not exclusively ios::trunc's job. Opening ofstream f("data.txt", ios::ate); truncates the file, because an output-only mode without ios::in maps onto the C mode "w". ios::ate preserves existing contents only when the mode also includes ios::in, as in fstream f("data.txt", ios::in | ios::out | ios::ate);. ios::app, by contrast, never truncates.

Error handling uses four state bits held in the stream, not return codes. goodbit means all is well, eofbit means end of input was reached, failbit means a logical failure such as a formatting mismatch or a failed open, and badbit means the stream is corrupt at the buffer level. The predicates are good(), eof(), fail() and bad(); rdstate() returns the whole state and clear() resets it, optionally to a value you supply. Testing a stream in a boolean context, as in while (fin >> x), reports whether failbit or badbit is set; eofbit on its own does not make a stream test false. This resolves the standard question: attempting an extraction with no data left sets eofbit and failbit together, and it is failbit that makes the stream test false, which is precisely why while (fin >> x) terminates cleanly and why the once-common while (!fin.eof()) loop processes the last item twice. After a deliberate read to end of file, clear() must be called before any repositioning will work. A stream can also be told to convert states into exceptions with fin.exceptions(ios::failbit | ios::badbit);, which then throws std::ios_base::failure.

Random access uses seekg and tellg for the get pointer and seekp and tellp for the put pointer. The two-argument form takes an offset and a direction, one of ios::beg, ios::cur or ios::end, so f.seekg(-20, ios::cur); moves the get pointer twenty bytes back from where it is, while f.seekg(20, ios::beg); is an absolute position and f.seekg(-1, ios::end); is one byte before the end. Negative offsets are meaningful only with cur and end. The record calculation is the standard worked example: with fixed-size records, the nth record counting from one begins at (n - 1) * sizeof(Record), so reading record 5 of a 40-byte record type is f.seekg(4 * 40, ios::beg); followed by f.read(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&rec), sizeof(rec));, and the number of records in the file is obtained by seeking to the end and dividing tellg() by sizeof(Record). One warning that questions exploit: on a single fstream object the get and put positions are one shared file position, so calling seekp also moves the read position; they are independent only when you have two separate stream objects open on the file. Binary read and write move raw bytes, which is safe for plain-data classes but not for objects owning pointers or carrying a vptr, since an address written today means nothing when read back.

Exam shape: MCQ items are mode-flag comparisons, stream-state reasoning and the seek direction constants. The conventional half asks for programs, typically write a class's objects to a binary file and read back a chosen record, or append to an existing file and count its records, so practise the open-check, the read loop and the seek arithmetic as code rather than as description.
facts: ifstream derives from istream, ofstream from ostream and fstream from iostream; all of them attach a filebuf and inherit the formatting and error state from basic_ios.
Default open modes are ios::in for ifstream, ios::out combined with ios::trunc for ofstream, and ios::in combined with ios::out for fstream, which requires the file to already exist.
ios::app appends every write to the end of the file whatever the pointer's position; ios::ate only seeks to the end once, at open time, after which writes go wherever the pointer is.
Opening an output-only stream with ios::ate and no ios::in still truncates the file, because the mode maps to C's "w"; ios::ate preserves contents only when ios::in is also present.
The stream state bits are goodbit, eofbit, failbit and badbit, queried with good(), eof(), fail(), bad() and rdstate(), and reset with clear().
A failed extraction at end of file sets both eofbit and failbit, and it is failbit that makes the stream test false in a boolean context; eofbit alone would not.
seekg and tellg move and report the get pointer, seekp and tellp the put pointer; the direction argument is ios::beg, ios::cur or ios::end, and negative offsets are meaningful only with cur and end.
On a single fstream object the get and put positions are one shared file position, so seekp also moves the read position; they are separate only across distinct stream objects.
With fixed-size records the nth record starts at byte offset (n - 1) * sizeof(Record), and the record count is tellg() at end of file divided by sizeof(Record).
setw affects only the next insertion and then resets, whereas precision, fill and the format flags persist until explicitly changed.
endl differs from the newline character only in that it flushes the stream's buffer; cerr is unit-buffered while clog is buffered.
traps: ios::app versus ios::ate: the difference is where writes go, not whether contents survive. app redirects every write to the end; ate only positions the pointer at open. A distractor saying app discards contents and ate preserves them is wrong on both halves.

Truncation is not exclusively ios::trunc's doing. Writing ofstream out("f.txt", ios::ate) to append silently empties the file, because output without ios::in opens in write mode; the working forms are ios::app or an fstream with ios::in | ios::out | ios::ate.

eofbit does not make a stream test false; failbit does. This is why while (!fin.eof()) reads one item too many and while (fin >> x) does not, and a distractor offering 'only eofbit is set and the stream remains usable' is the trap.

seekg(20, ios::beg) is an absolute position, not a relative move. Moving backwards from the current position is seekg(-20, ios::cur), and seekp on an ifstream is meaningless because there is no put pointer to move.
After hitting end of file you must call clear() before a seek will take effect; candidates write the seek, see it do nothing, and blame the offset arithmetic.

Writing an object with virtual functions or pointer members using write and sizeof stores a vptr and raw addresses that are meaningless on read-back; binary object I/O is valid only for plain-data classes.
mnem: app appends every write, ate only arrives at the end. Beginning, current, end are the only three seek origins, and only current and end take a negative offset.

def: Exception handling separates the detection of a run-time error from its treatment: a throw expression creates an exception object and abandons the current path, the stack is unwound with destructors run for every fully constructed automatic object, and the first matching catch handler of an enclosing try block takes over. std::string is the standard library's dynamically sized, mutable, value-semantic character sequence, and it is also the canonical source of thrown standard exceptions.
exp:
The mechanism has three named parts and the syllabus lists two of them separately. The throwing mechanism: throw x; copy-initialises an exception object from x into storage the implementation controls, so the object outlives the scope that threw it, and control leaves the block. Between the throw point and the handler the run time performs stack unwinding, destroying every automatic object that had been fully constructed, in reverse order of construction. This is exactly why RAII matters: a lock or a file handle owned by a local object is released correctly on the exception path with no cleanup code written anywhere, whereas a raw new whose delete sits after the throw point leaks. If no handler is found anywhere on the call chain the exception is uncaught and std::terminate is called, which by default calls abort. Since C++11 a destructor is implicitly noexcept, so an exception escaping a destructor also calls terminate, and this is the reason for the rule that destructors must not throw.

The catching mechanism is the part where an exam item can be won or lost, because handler selection is not overload resolution. Handlers are examined strictly in the order they are written, and the first one whose type can match the thrown object wins; there is no ranking of a more derived handler as a better match. So if a try block lists catch (const std::exception&) before catch (const std::out_of_range&) and an out_of_range is thrown, the std::exception handler runs, because out_of_range derives from exception and the base handler was written first. The code is not ill-formed and the program does not terminate; it merely does the wrong thing, and compilers warn about it. The rule that follows is to order handlers most derived first and most general last, with catch (...) as the final handler if it appears at all. Only one handler runs for a given throw; handlers do not chain.

Catch by reference, conventionally const reference, for class types. A by-value handler copy-initialises its parameter from the exception object, so a derived exception is sliced down to the handler's base type and its overriding what() and any derived state are lost. By-value handlers are legal, which is what makes this a design rule rather than a compile error. Related: rethrowing with a bare throw; inside a handler propagates the original exception object unchanged, whereas writing throw e; where e is the caught base reference throws a fresh, sliced copy. The standard hierarchy rooted at std::exception, with its virtual what() returning const char*, splits into logic_error, with invalid_argument, domain_error, length_error and out_of_range beneath it, and runtime_error, with range_error, overflow_error and underflow_error; std::bad_alloc from a failed new and std::bad_cast from a failed dynamic_cast on a reference sit alongside them. Custom exception classes should derive from one of these and override what(). Dynamic exception specifications of the form throw(Type) are obsolete and have been removed from the language; noexcept is the current annotation, and violating it calls terminate rather than looking for a handler.

std::string, declared in the string header, is basic_string specialised for char. It is a value type: assignment and passing copy the characters, unlike Java or C# where a string variable is a reference to an immutable object, and it is mutable in place. Its storage is contiguous, and since C++11 both c_str() and data() return a null-terminated buffer; implementations commonly keep short strings inside the object itself under the small-string optimisation, which is why size() and capacity() differ and why capacity may be non-zero for an empty string. size() and length() are exact synonyms. Comparison with == and the relational operators is lexicographic by character value, compare() returns a negative value, zero or a positive value, and + concatenates. The searching functions, find, rfind, find_first_of and their relatives, return std::string::npos on failure, and npos is a size_type, meaning unsigned, so a test such as if (s.find(t) < 0) is always false and the only correct test is against std::string::npos.

The two halves of this leaf meet at bounds checking, which is a direct exam item. For a string holding five characters, s.at(9) performs a range check, fails it and throws std::out_of_range, an exception you can catch. s[9] performs no check at all: it is undefined behaviour, which in practice may return garbage, may appear to work, and may crash, but is not an exception and cannot be caught. The same split runs through the library generally, vector::at against vector::operator[] being the other standard pair. substr also throws out_of_range if the starting position exceeds the size, and stoi throws invalid_argument when no conversion is possible and out_of_range when the value does not fit.

Exam shape: MCQ items are handler ordering, catch-by-reference reasoning and the at versus subscript distinction. The conventional half is explicitly code-shaped here, since write a program that defines its own exception class derived from std::exception and demonstrates throwing, catching and rethrowing, or write a program using string functions to reverse and search a line of text, are both standard long questions; marks are lost by omitting the const reference in the handler and by forgetting that only the first matching handler runs.
facts: throw copy-initialises an exception object that outlives the throwing scope, and stack unwinding then destroys every fully constructed automatic object between the throw point and the handler, in reverse order of construction.

Catch handlers are examined in the order written and the first type that matches wins; there is no preference for a more derived handler, so a base handler written first will catch a derived exception.
Only one handler executes per thrown exception, and catch (...) matches anything and must therefore be written last.
Catching a class type by value slices a derived exception down to the handler's parameter type; catching by const reference preserves the dynamic type and avoids the copy.
A bare throw; inside a handler rethrows the original exception object, whereas throw e; on the caught reference throws a new, sliced copy.
An uncaught exception calls std::terminate, which by default calls abort; the same happens if an exception escapes a destructor, since destructors are implicitly noexcept since C++11.

std::exception is the base of the standard hierarchy and supplies virtual what(); logic_error covers invalid_argument, domain_error, length_error and out_of_range, while runtime_error covers range_error, overflow_error and underflow_error.
Dynamic exception specifications written as throw(Type) have been removed from the language; noexcept is the current form and violating it calls terminate.
std::string has value semantics and is mutable, size() and length() are synonyms, storage is contiguous, and c_str() and data() return a null-terminated buffer.
The string search functions return std::string::npos on failure, and npos is an unsigned size_type, so the failure test must compare against npos rather than against a negative number.

std::string::at performs a bounds check and throws std::out_of_range, while operator[] is unchecked and out-of-range use is undefined behaviour; substr throws out_of_range if the start position exceeds the size.
traps: Handler order is textual order, not best match. With catch (const std::exception&) written before catch (const std::out_of_range&), an out_of_range is caught by the base handler; the answer is not 'the more derived handler wins', not 'both run', and not 'the program terminates'.

at() throws and operator[] does not. For a five-character string, at(9) throws std::out_of_range while s[9] is undefined behaviour, so a distractor saying both throw, or that the subscript returns the terminating null, is wrong.

Catching by value is legal code, so the reason to catch by reference is slicing and the loss of the derived type, not a compiler rejection; the by-value handler compiles and then quietly does the wrong thing.

Rethrowing with throw e; from a handler taking a base reference is not equivalent to throw;. The first creates a sliced copy of the base type, the second propagates the original object with its dynamic type intact.
npos is unsigned, so if (pos < 0) after a find never fires however clearly it reads; the comparison must be pos == std::string::npos.

Stack unwinding runs destructors for automatic objects only. Memory obtained with new and not owned by an object is not reclaimed when an exception passes through, which is the point of RAII and of smart pointers.
mnem: Handlers are read top to bottom, so derived first and catch-all last. at throws, subscript trusts you.
